issues.title: PE header fields parsed as signed and not unsinged
issues.description_message:
The PE header fields are parsed as signed and not unsigned see: https://github.com/NationalSecurityAgency/ghidra/blob/49c2010b63b56c8f20845f3970fedd95d003b1e9/Ghidra/Features/Base/src/main/java/ghidra/app/util/bin/format/pe/SectionHeader.java#L493

If now e.g. `virtualSize` or `rawDataSize => 0x10000000` then the read in value becomes negative. This means sections larger than `0x0fffffff` bytes can not be read or allocated. Impact of other header fields becoming negative is unknown.

Two possible solutions:
1. read everything as unsigned into the next bigger data type
2. handle overflows better, e.g. check consequences of values overflowing

As this doesn't seem to cause immediate problems (>2GiB PE files are rare and also the other fields seem to rarely reach overflow limit, plus PE parsing seems to work just fine as is) I'd rate the severity of this very low. However as #327 could lead to frustrating symptoms. Hence, I open this issue.

Other testcases to harden the PE loader see: https://github.com/NationalSecurityAgency/ghidra/pull/418#issuecomment-486889500

issues.title: [M68000] Add Motorola CPU32 (683xx) support
issues.description_message:
Currently Ghidra lacks CPU32 (Motorola/Freescale 683xx) processor support.

CPU32 instruction set is same as 68020, with exception of:

**The folllowing instructions are CPU32 specific:**
 - LPSTOP  — low-power stop
 - TBLxxx — table lookup and interpolate

**The following M68020 instructions are NOT implemented on the CPU32:**
 - BFxxx — Bit Field Instructions (BFCHG, BFCLR, BFEXTS, BFEXTU, BFFFOBFINS, BFSET, BFTST)
 - CALLM, RTM — Call Module, Return Module
 - CAS, CAS2 — Compare and Set (Read-Modify-Write Instructions)
 - cpxxx — Coprocessor Instructions (cpBcc, cpDBcc, cpGEN, cp RESTORE,cpSAVE, cpScc, cpTRAPcc)
 - PACK, UNPK — Pack, Unpack BCD Instructions

I have made some effort to try and add CPU32 instructions in my [fork](https://github.com/dzidaV8/ghidra/tree/master/Ghidra/Processors/68000/data/languages).

[CPU32 Reference Manual](https://www.nxp.com/docs/en/reference-manual/CPU32RM.pdf)

issues.title: SLEIGH: 64-bit signed token field constraints do not compile
issues.description_message:
**Describe the bug**
64-bit signed token field constraints cause a compiler error.

**To Reproduce**
This file:

```
define endian=little;
define alignment=1;
define space ram type=ram_space size=8 default;

define token foo (64)
    bar = (0,63)
; 

:baz is bar=0x1234 {}
```

Gives the following error:

```
$ sleigh problem.slaspec
...
WARN  1 NOP constructors found (SleighCompile)  
WARN  Use -n switch to list each individually (SleighCompile)  
Error: Equal constraint is impossible to match: for table "instruction" constructor from problem.slaspec:9
ERROR No output produced (SleighCompile)  
```

I believe this is because the following check does not handle unsigned longs properly:

https://github.com/NationalSecurityAgency/ghidra/blob/687ce7f529d17f0fa215c2d8193b39b6ea8f636a/Ghidra/Framework/SoftwareModeling/src/main/java/ghidra/pcodeCPort/slghpatexpress/EqualEquation.java#L29-L56

`TokenField.maxValue()` is implemented as:

https://github.com/NationalSecurityAgency/ghidra/blob/687ce7f529d17f0fa215c2d8193b39b6ea8f636a/Ghidra/Framework/SoftwareModeling/src/main/java/ghidra/pcodeCPort/slghpatexpress/TokenField.java#L54-L60

So the maximum value here is `~0` (*which is actually -1 since Java `long`s are signed*), but is compared with the operand using `val <= lhsmax` rather than `val.compareUnsigned(lhsmax) <= 0`. I would open a PR to fix this, but I am worried this is only one instance of the issue and am not super familiar with Ghidra so I don't know how to find/fix them all.

**Expected behavior**
The code should successfully compile.

**Environment:**
 - OS: macOS 10.14.6
 - Java Version: 12.0.1
 - Ghidra Version: 9.1.2

issues.title: Section names out of bounds causes parsing error
issues.description_message:
Section names can be specified as an offset into the string table using "/[OFFSET]" as name for a section. Choosing an out-of-bounds offset will cause Ghidra to not parse the file as a PE at all. A maliciously crafted PE file can choose such an offset to evade analysis.

Here is how to create an example .exe:
```bash
echo '#include <stdio.h>
void main(void) { printf("hello world"); }' > a.c
x86_64-w64-mingw32-gcc a.c -o a.exe
strip --strip-debug --keep-section-symbols --keep-file-symbols a.exe
sed -i "s/.text\x00\x00\x00/\/9999999/g" a.exe
```

issues.title: Disassembly/Decompile manipulation due to loading discrepancy in PE
issues.description_message:
Microsoft specifies that for executable images the PointerToRawData must be a multiple of the FileAlignment.
However, Windows does in fact load executables where this is untrue.
In fact, Windows will round down to the nearest multiple of 0x200. Please note that while the default FileAlignment is 0x200, Windows will round to a multiple of 0x200 regardless of the FileAlignment.


As an example section take:
.text:
    - PointerToRawData: 0x820
    - VirtualAddress: RVA:0x1000

Windows will round down to 0x800 and start reading there, but Ghidra starts reading at 0x820.

Now assume that at 0x800 a malicious function is located and at 0x820 a harmless one.

This means that for this maliciously crafted PE file, Ghidra will show the user at RVA:0x1000 the function that lies at 0x820. In reality the function at 0x800 is executed at RVA:0x1000.


This means that a reverser can be tricked into looking at a function that is actually not executed, while the function that is executed is not visible to the reverser at all.

Here is an illustration:

On disk:
```
    0x800  41 41 41 41 41 41 41 41 41 41 41 41 41 41 41 41  |AAAAAAAAAAAAAAAA|
    0x810  42 42 42 42 42 42 42 42 42 42 42 42 42 42 42 42  |BBBBBBBBBBBBBBBB|
    0x820  43 43 43 43 43 43 43 43 43 43 43 43 43 43 43 43  |CCCCCCCCCCCCCCCC|
    0x830  44 44 44 44 44 44 44 44 44 44 44 44 44 44 44 44  |DDDDDDDDDDDDDDDD|
    0x840  45 45 45 45 45 45 45 45 45 45 45 45 45 45 45 45  |EEEEEEEEEEEEEEEE|
    0x850  ...
```

On Windows:
```
RVA:0x1000  41 41 41 41 41 41 41 41 41 41 41 41 41 41 41 41  |AAAAAAAAAAAAAAAA|
RVA:0x1010  42 42 42 42 42 42 42 42 42 42 42 42 42 42 42 42  |BBBBBBBBBBBBBBBB|
RVA:0x1020  43 43 43 43 43 43 43 43 43 43 43 43 43 43 43 43  |CCCCCCCCCCCCCCCC|
RVA:0x1030  ...
```

In Ghidra:
```
RVA:0x1000  43 43 43 43 43 43 43 43 43 43 43 43 43 43 43 43  |CCCCCCCCCCCCCCCC|
RVA:0x1010  44 44 44 44 44 44 44 44 44 44 44 44 44 44 44 44  |DDDDDDDDDDDDDDDD|
RVA:0x1020  45 45 45 45 45 45 45 45 45 45 45 45 45 45 45 45  |EEEEEEEEEEEEEEEE|
RVA:0x1030  ...
```

As this is a parsing bug, the disassembler view and the decompiler view are affected.

Also note that when a PointerToRawData is 0x0, no data will be loaded (uninitialized section). But the check if PointerToRawData is 0x0, is before rounding down. So in the case where PointerToRawData is between 0x001 and 0x1ff, Windows will load from offset 0x0.

An exe file for testing with a different FileAlignment can be generated like this:
```bash
x86_64-w64-mingw32-gcc a.c -Wl,--file-alignment=0x1000 -o out.exe
```

For testing these behaviors described one can change the PointerToRawData in for example PE-bear and see how the section is loaded in x64dbg.


These behaviors were tested on Windows 11 with 32-Bit and 64-Bit executables, with 0x200, 0x800 and 0x1000 as FileAlignment.

Similar behavior for SizeOfRawData: #9171

issues.title: Low-level Error: assignment to constant
issues.description_message:
**Describe the bug**

RISC-V binaries including instructions like ` amoadd.d  zero,a5,(a4)` cause the decompiler to quit with the Low-level Error: assignment to constant.  The decompiler throws this error when an attempt is made to write to a constant Varnode, likely a Varnode holding the constant value '0'.

Reproduce by running the attached file as a decompiler datatest.

**Expected behavior**

The RISC-V register r0 - aka `zero` - is treated as a discard sink rather than the constant `0` when used in a destination register context

**Attachments**

The attached xml file can be used to reproduce the error in the decompiler datatest context.
[dpdk_sample_4_save.xml](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/27974391/dpdk_sample_4_save.xml)

The datatest script for this will be something like:

```text
restore test_data/dpdk_sample_4_save.xml
map function 0x2879b2 rte_vhost_notify_guest
parse line extern void rte_vhost_notify_guest(ulong param_1, ulong param_2);
load function rte_vhost_notify_guest
decompile rte_vhost_notify_guest
print C
print raw
```

**Environment (please complete the following information):**
 - OS: Fedora 44
 - Java Version: NA
 - Ghidra Version: 12.2-DEV
 - Ghidra Origin: locally built

**Additional context**

Many RISC-V instructions define two patterns, one matching for `rd=r0` and the other for any other destination register. 



 We could do the same thing for the `amo*` instructions.   There may be a more elegant way of expressing discard semantics for register r0, perhaps involving this line in `riscv.table.sinc`:

    rdL: zero is r0711 & zero & op0711=0 { export 0:8; }

issues.title: Hexagon variadic calling convention does not model stack varargs correctly
issues.description_message:
Ghidra’s Hexagon calling convention currently does not correctly model variadic functions such as `printf`, `sprintf`, `snprintf`, and `vsnprintf`.

Per the Hexagon ABI, fixed parameters are passed normally, but variadic arguments are passed on the stack. In practice, this causes the decompiler to miss or mis-handle extra arguments unless the user manually applies custom signature overrides at each call site.

A downstream Hexagon SLEIGH project fixed this by adding separate variadic calling conventions such as `vararg1`, `vararg2`, and `vararg3`:

https://github.com/CUB3D/ghidra-hexagon-sleigh/pull/30

It would be helpful if upstream Ghidra’s Hexagon processor support could model this behavior directly, or provide a generic way for `.cspec` calling conventions to say: “after N fixed arguments, place variadic arguments on the stack.”

issues.title: x86-64: `RCL`/`RCR` should set `OF` flag when masked count is 0 or 1
issues.description_message:
**Describe the bug**
According to the Intel SDM, the `RCL`/`RCR` instructions set the OF flag when the masked count is 0 or 1:

> The OF flag is **defined only for the 1-bit rotates**; it is undefined in all other cases (**except RCL and RCR instructions only: a zero-bit rotate does nothing**, that is affects no flags).

Ghidra does not update the OF flag at all.

**To Reproduce**
Load the program compiled from the assembly below into Ghidra.
Navigate to the function `run`.
The decompilation window will show something like:

```c
undefined1  [16] run(undefined8 param_1,undefined8 param_2,ulong param_3)

{
  undefined1 auVar1 [16];
  
  auVar1._8_8_ = 0;
  auVar1._0_8_ = param_3;
  return auVar1 << 0x40;
}
```

When toggling off "eliminate dead code", Ghidra will show an if (true) or if (false) branch that makes it seem like the syscall is never executed.

**Expected behavior**
The decompilation of the `run` function should show an always-executed `syscall`.
You can verify this by running the binary, and confirming that it prints a message "Everything OK" to stdout.

**Attachments**
A minimal program to reproduce:
```asm
section .data
    msg db "Everything OK", 10
    len equ $ - msg

section .text
    global _start

run:
    mov eax, 0xffffffff
    ; Overflows, so OF=1
    add eax, 0x80000000
    mov eax, 0
    clc
    mov ecx, 1

    ; Uncomment exactly one:
    rcl eax, cl
    ; rcr eax, cl
    ; Both should set OF=0

    jno ok
    ret

ok:
    mov rsi, msg
    mov rdx, len
    mov rax, 1
    mov rdi, 1
    syscall
    ret

_start:
    call run
    mov rax, 60
    xor rdi, rdi
    syscall
    ret
```

The program can be compiled with `nasm -f elf64 -o test.o test.s`, then linked with `ld -o test test.o`.
It will print "Everything OK" with a syscall in the run function when executed,
but Ghidra will incorrectly consider this syscall to be unreachable.

**Environment (please complete the following information):**
 - OS: Ubuntu 26.04
 - Java Version: openjdk 11.0.31 2026-04-21
 - Ghidra Version: 12.1.2
 - Ghidra Origin: flatpak

issues.title: Debugger (gdb): ghidragdb cannot map MIPS ISA-level architectures (e.g. mips:isa64r2), falls back to DATA64
issues.description_message:
**Describe the bug**

`ghidragdb` maps gdb's BFD architecture name to a Ghidra language via `language_map` in `Ghidra/Debug/Debugger-agent-gdb/src/main/py/src/ghidragdb/arch.py`. The MIPS entries cover only specific legacy CPU names — `mips:3000`, `mips:4000`, `mips:5000`, `mips:micromips` — and omit the ISA-level names (`mips:isa32[r2/r6]`, `mips:isa64[r2/r6]`) that gdb selects for ISA-generic MIPS targets.

gdb reports the ISA-level name automatically from an ordinary MIPS ELF — no custom target description is required. For a stock big-endian MIPS64R2 executable:

```
(gdb) file mips64_hello_static
(gdb) show architecture
The target architecture is set to "auto" (currently "mips:isa64r2").
```

When the Debugger connects to such a target, `compute_ghidra_language()` does not find `mips:isa64r2` in `language_map` and falls back to `DATA:BE:64:default`. That data language has no program counter, so the trace attaches but register/PC handling is broken:

- Register hover in the Listing: `platform must have a program counter`
- On stop: `gdb.GdbError: Cannot convert status's value: '<unavailable>'` (from `commands.putreg` → `arch.map_value`)
- The log shows `Using the DATA64 compiler map`; the Decompiler view stays empty.

The legacy `mips:NNNN` names still work and are unaffected — the map is simply missing the ISA-level family.

**To Reproduce**

1. Have a MIPS64 (or MIPS32r2+) target where `(gdb) show architecture` reports an ISA-level name, e.g. `mips:isa64r2`.
2. Connect Ghidra's Debugger (gdb). The trace is created as `DATA:BE:64:default`; registers cannot be read and the Decompiler stays empty.

**Expected behavior**

Map the `mips:isaNN[rN]` names to the matching `MIPS:*:32/64:default` languages, the same way `mips:5000` already maps to `MIPS:BE:64:default`.

**Environment**

- Ghidra 12.1.2 (arch.py unchanged on `master`)
- gdb-multiarch 17.1; big-endian MIPS64R2 target

**Workaround**

`set ghidra-language MIPS:BE:64:default` before the trace starts.

**Suggested fix**

Add the ISA-level names to `language_map` in `ghidragdb/arch.py` (pull request to follow).

issues.title: Delay-load imports: enumeration from IAT vs INT when lengths differ - intended behaviour?
issues.description_message:
When a delay-load descriptor's Import Name Table (INT) and Import Address Table (IAT) have different lengths, Ghidra appears to enumerate imports from the IAT, where several other PE tools enumerate from the INT. I'd like to understand whether this is a deliberate design choice, and how the loader is intended to handle an INT/IAT length mismatch.

## Observed behaviour

Testing with a minimal PE32+ binary whose single delay-load descriptor has:

- INT: three entries (Foo, Bar, Baz) + null terminator
- IAT: two entries (Foo, Bar) + null terminator

Ghidra 12.1 (headless, default analysis) enumerates two delay-load imports:

```plaintext
DDI: delay_dir_parsed=true datatype=ImgDelayDescr
DDI: external_library=TEST.DLL
DDI: external_symbol=TEST.DLL!Foo
DDI: external_symbol=TEST.DLL!Bar
DDI: external_symbol_count=2
```

(Output from a small postscript walking `getSymbolTable().getExternalSymbols()`.)

*Note: datatype=ImgDelayDescr - Ghidra parsed the descriptor structure cleanly; the divergence is purely in which array it uses for the import count, not a parse failure.*

For comparison, on the same binary:

- dumpbin 14.44 enumerates 3 (from INT; the third shown with a null IAT address)
- pefile 2024.8.26 enumerates 3 (from INT)

So Ghidra reports two imports where dumpbin and pefile report three. The difference appears to be that Ghidra walks the IAT to determine the import count, while the others walk the INT.

## Why I'm asking

I'm studying how PE parsers handle malformed/edge-case delay-load structures, using single-anomaly test binaries (this one differs from a well-formed binary only in the INT/IAT length mismatch; a well-formed control with matching INT/IAT is enumerated identically by all tools, Ghidra included all 3 imports).

The PE specification doesn't state which array is authoritative when the two disagree, so I don't think any tool is strictly wrong here. I'm trying to understand the different implementation choices. Ghidra's choice to key off the IAT is defensible; I'd just like to know:

1. Is IAT-based enumeration intentional for delay-load imports, or a side effect of how the loader walks the descriptor?
2. How does Ghidra intend to handle an INT/IAT length mismatch; is it treated as malformed, or is one array simply taken as authoritative by design?
3. Would it be useful for Ghidra to surface the mismatch (e.g., a bookmark or log warning) when the arrays disagree, given that the divergence is silent today?

## Not a bug report

To be clear, I'm not reporting this as a defect. Ghidra parses the descriptor cleanly and produces a reasonable result. On a well-formed binary Ghidra's output matches the other tools exactly. This is a question about intended behaviour on a specifically malformed edge case, which the PE spec underspecifies. I've also raised the underlying spec ambiguity with the PE format documentation: https://github.com/MicrosoftDocs/win32/pull/2202

## Reproduction

Minimal PE32+ test binary and the headless dump postscript are available at https://github.com/malx-labs/pe-delayload-divergence. Happy to provide the fixture directly if useful. Ghidra version 12.1 PUBLIC, default headless analysis options.

Thanks, genuinely curious how the loader team thinks about this case.
